bodyMarkdown:
## The idea in plain language

Scheduling puzzles are timetables with gaps. Five people, five days, some rules about who cannot go on which day.

It is the same grid technique as any matching puzzle, with one extra feature: time has an order. 'Before' and 'after' constrain things that 'different from' does not.

## What is actually going on

Build a grid of slots against entities. Mark the impossible cells from the negative clues first — these are usually generous and cut the space down fast.

Then apply the ordering clues. 'A is scheduled before B' means A cannot take the last slot and B cannot take the first, which is often an immediate elimination people miss.

Watch for clues about gaps ('three days after') versus mere order ('some day after'). And check whether every slot must be filled, or whether some can be empty — that changes the counting.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: Four presentations run Monday to Thursday, one per day. P is before Q. R is on Wednesday. P is not on Monday. When is P?
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
R takes Wednesday, leaving Monday, Tuesday and Thursday for P, Q and S.

P is not on Monday, so P is Tuesday or Thursday.

P must be before Q, so P cannot be Thursday — nothing would be left after it.

So P is on Tuesday.

formulaCards.title: Ordering eliminations
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: 'A before B' immediately rules A out of the last slot and B out of the first.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: With four slots and A before B, A can only be in slots 1 to 3.

formulaCards.title: Grid first, order second
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: Apply negative and fixed clues to the grid first, then layer the ordering constraints onto what remains.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: Fixing one entity to Wednesday shrinks the problem before any ordering logic is needed.

commonTraps: Missing the automatic first-and-last eliminations that any ordering clue produces.
Assuming every slot is filled when the puzzle allows empty ones.
